gambangkromong.window: Mid-18th century beginnings (Kapitan Nie Hoe Kong, in office 1736–1740) as a gambang orchestra; named gambang kromong once the kromong was added in the early 20th century; peak of popularity around 1937; still played across greater Jakarta, on record in Benyamin S. and Ida Royani's Betawi songs, 1990s cassettes, the Smithsonian Folkways field album of 1991 and digital releases to 2024.
gambangkromong.sound: The orchestra of Jakarta's Betawi and Chinese-Peranakan communities: the wooden gambang xylophone and the kromong gong-chime with gong, kendang drums, suling flute and kecrek, under the Chinese bowed strings sukong, tehyan and kongahyan carrying the melody, in a Chinese pentatonic scale. Its repertoire runs from instrumental phobin and classical lagu dalem sung by cokek singers to the popular lagu sayur (Jali-Jali, Stambul, Cente Manis) for cokek dancing and lenong theatre; 'gambang kromong kombinasi' adds guitar, bass, organ, saxophone and drums.
markers: The nasal, sliding melody of the Chinese two-string fiddles (tehyan, kongahyan, sukong) over a wooden xylophone
The ringing kromong gong-chime and gong marking the cycle, with kendang drum for dancing
A Chinese pentatonic tune sung in Betawi Malay, often a playful pantun-style lagu sayur such as Jali-Jali or a Stambul
fits: Music of Indonesia, Vol. 3: Music from the Outskirts of Jakarta: Gambang Kromong (album)
near: Balinese gamelan gambang: a sacred bronze-and-wood ensemble of the same name, but with no kromong, no Chinese bowed strings and no Betawi songs
The best-known kroncong song: ukulele-and-guitar kroncong from Central Java, sharing Jakarta's mixed roots but not the gambang, kromong or Chinese fiddles
A Javanese karawitan gendhing named after the gambang, played by a Central Javanese gamelan in slendro or pelog, not a Betawi-Chinese gambang kromong orchestra

shokaandgunka.window: 1881 to 1945: from the first Ministry of Education school songbook (Shōgaku shōkashū, first volume dated 1881) and one of the first composed gunka (Battōtai, 1885) to Japan's surrender. Monbushō shōka filled school textbooks from 1910 to 1944 (the subject itself became 'music' in 1941); gunka boomed in the wars of 1894-95 and 1904-05 and were mass-produced on records from 1931, then banned under the Occupation until 1952. Re-recorded by choirs and singers ever since.
shokaandgunka.sound: The Western-style songs Meiji Japan built for its schools and its army: simple, singable melodies in a major key, at first borrowed from German and American school songs, hymns and Scottish airs and given Japanese words, then newly composed by Japanese musicians from 1910. School shōka are sung by children's or mixed choirs with piano or small orchestra, about the seasons, the home village and diligence; gunka are marching songs in four-four time with a brass band of trumpets, trombones, snare and cymbals behind unison male voices, telling the story of a battle or a fallen comrade, and from the 1930s they became record-company hits with star singers.
markers: Plain major-key tunes that a whole class or regiment can sing in unison, many on the five-note yonanuki scale
Children's or mixed choir with piano or small orchestra for school songs; unison male voices over a military brass band in march time for gunka
Long strophic texts in formal literary Japanese: the seasons and the home village, or a battle, a hero and a dead comrade, verse after verse
fits: 中野忠晴/松平晃/伊藤久男/佐々木章
near: A 1940 Columbia hit by the same record industry and the same war years, but a sentimental popular song (kayōkyoku) about a lakeside inn, written for the record market, not for the school or the army
海上自衛隊横須賀音楽隊
The same melody as the sung gunka "Gunkan", played by the Maritime Self-Defense Force band as an instrumental march with no words: band music, not a song

nurthi.window: 1879 onward (C. Don Bastian's Rolina, per the Sunday Times; the tree's 1886 is John de Silva's Ramayanaya per English Wikipedia); commercial nurthi stage ended with silent cinema (no year read); revived from 1978 at the restored Tower Hall and by the Tower Hall Theatre Foundation
nurthi.sound: The song of the Sinhala nurthi stage, a musical theatre born in Colombo from the Parsi touring companies (Elphinstone Dramatic Company, 1880s): Sinhala verses set to Hindustani and Gujarati stage melodies, with raga and tala chosen to fit each scene's sentiment (rasa), accompanied by harmonium, violin and dhol. John de Silva's plays on Sinhala history and Buddhist legend (Siri Sangabo, 1903) gave its best-known songs, such as Danno Budunge.
markers: A North Indian (Hindustani or Parsi-theatre) melody carrying Sinhala verses
Harmonium leading, with violin and dhol drum behind the voice
Solo stage song in character from a play on kings, gods or Buddhist history, in a raga chosen for the scene's mood
near: A song from the 1947 film Asokamala with original melodies by Mohammed Gauss (who had written for nurthi plays): a film song, not a stage-play song
Sung by a nurthi actress in Kadawunu Poronduwa, the first Sinhala talkie (1947), made by the Minerva stage troupe: it is a film song issued with the film, not a nurthi stage song

funana.window: c. 1900 onward (tree date; Wikipedia's oral tradition puts the accordion's arrival on Santiago at the start of the 20th century, with no document to prove it; the name dates from the 1960s-70s; first records found 1978)
funana.sound: The accordion dance music of rural Santiago, Cape Verde: a diatonic button accordion (gaita) carrying the melody, bass and chords, a ferrinho iron scraper struck with a knife driving a fast two-beat pulse, and a Creole singer trading verses and refrain with accordion solos between them. Once banned in the colonial capital, it was electrified by Bulimundo around 1980 (guitar, bass, drums, synthesizer in place of the gaita), spread across the islands and abroad with Finaçon, and turned back to gaita and ferrinho with Ferro Gaita from 1997; danced in couples with quick alternating knee flexes.
markers: A diatonic button accordion (gaita) playing a running melody and solos between the verses
The scrape of a ferrinho iron bar struck with a knife on a fast two-beat pulse
A Creole singer trading proverb-laden verses with a refrain, in a tempo from andante to vivace
near: A slow, melancholy morna of emigration and longing over guitar and cavaquinho, the prestige urban song of the islands, not the fast gaita-and-ferrinho dance of rural Santiago
A coladeira: guitar and cavaquinho strumming the mãozada with a cycle-of-fifths harmony from morna, sung by the same band that recorded the funaná Codjeta, but without gaita or ferrinho

porro.window: Band porro took shape in the Sinú and the savannas of Córdoba, Sucre and Bolívar in the late 19th century (the word 'porro' comes into use then; tree date 1900); orchestral porro spread nationally and abroad from the 1940s to the 1970s; band porro lives on in festivals (San Pelayo, since 1977) and in revival records (2010).
porro.sound: Dance music of Colombia's Caribbean plains, born where gaita flute-and-drum groups met military wind bands: a banda pelayera of trumpets, clarinets, trombones and bombardino (euphonium) over bombo, snare and cymbals, in cut time (2/2). The trumpet leads the 'porro' section, the clarinet takes over in the 'bozá' while the bombo player beats a stick on the drum's rim (porro palitiao of the Sinú); in porro tapao of the savannas the bombo player muffles the far head with his hand. From the 1940s big orchestras such as Lucho Bermúdez's and Pacho Galán's dressed it for the ballroom.
markers: A brass band of trumpets, clarinets and bombardino trading call-and-response phrases
A bass drum (bombo) and snare driving a quick cut-time (2/2) march-like pulse, with cymbal crashes
A clarinet-led 'bozá' section over the dry click of a stick on the drum's rim
Instrumental or sung dance pieces for couples, often named after people and towns of Córdoba and Bolívar
near: Labelled a cumbia on the same compilation that labels Lucho Bermúdez's peers' tracks as porros: the cumbia rhythm with its gaita and drum roots, not the brass-band porro of the Sinú bands
A champeta (the title says so) on a porro revival album: the Cartagena dance music of picós and African guitar pop, not porro's wind band

changga.window: 1896 to the late 1920s (the first changga of 1896; patriotic and school changga until about 1910, pushed underground by the colonial ban; yuhaeng changga, the popular songs of the 1920s, until the genres split in the 1930s)
changga.sound: Korea's first Western-style songs: simple melodies in Western major and minor scales, very often borrowed (Protestant hymns, Scottish and American tunes such as Auld Lang Syne and Georgia March, Japan's Railway Song), set to Korean words in fixed syllable counts, 4·4 at first and 7·5 later, and sung verse after verse in unison by schoolchildren, church congregations and independence volunteers. Words urge study, strength and independence. In the 1920s yuhaeng changga carried the same plain melodic style into songs of parting and sorrow, such as 희망가 and the waltz 사의 찬미.
markers: A plain hymn-like or marching Western melody, often a borrowed foreign tune, sung in Korean
Many verses to one short tune, the lyrics in fixed syllable counts (4·4, later 7·5)
Words of exhortation, urging the young to study, grow strong and win independence (학도야 학도야), or in the 1920s a lament on a hard world
near: Korean-composed pentatonic yuhaengga of 1932, called a milestone of trot: the step from borrowed Western changga tunes to the new popular song
The changga 희망가 recast as 1970s folk rock by a singer-songwriter with acoustic guitar; the song is changga, the recording belongs to t'ong guitar folk

sudanesehaqiba.window: 1920s onward (Omdurman's new urban song of the 1920s and 1930s, on Cairo-made 78s from the late 1920s; named 'haqiba' in the 1940s after Radio Omdurman's Hageebat al-Fann programme, and sung by later haqiba singers ever since)
sudanesehaqiba.sound: Omdurman's first secular urban song: a lead singer answered by a chorus, carried at first only by the riq or tar frame drum and handclaps, with melodies taken from madeeh praise singing and set to new love and homeland poems; pentatonic, close to Sufi praise chant in poetic form, sung at weddings and social gatherings, and from the late 1920s sometimes joined by violin, accordion or piano on record.
markers: A solo voice with a chorus that claps and echoes its main lines
Only the riq or tar frame drum and handclaps for accompaniment, no orchestra
Love and homeland poems sung to madeeh-derived pentatonic tunes
fits: حقيبة الفن - ميرغني المأمون وأحمد حسن جمعة (album)
near: Post-haqiba modern song: al-Kashif left the riq-and-chorus haqiba manner for strings and Western instruments; a patriotic song of the late 1950s
Same singer's golden-age string-section song, reissued on Ostinato's violins-and-synths compilation; it grew out of haqiba but is no longer haqiba

twoubadou.window: Early 20th century onward (tree date 1920; no page gives a year). Kandjo (1879–1947) set the archetype; on record from Trio Select's first album in 1960; a commercial revival from the late 1990s (Mizik Mizik's Blakawout, Haitiando, Haiti Twoubadou) continues today.
twoubadou.sound: Haitian guitar-based song brought back from the Cuban cane fields by migrant cutters: one or two acoustic guitars, maracas or a graj scraper, a tanbou drum and a large lamellophone (manibula) playing the bass, with a pair of voices singing simple two-part verse-and-chorus songs about the bitterness and humour of love, often risqué. Played by small combos in clubs, restaurants, hotels and at patron-saint feasts, it sits close to Cuban son and mixes it with Haitian mereng.
markers: Two acoustic guitars trading Cuban-style lines over a light, swaying dance beat
Maracas or a graj scraper and a hand drum, with a thumb-piano (manibula) bass instead of a bass guitar
Two voices in Haitian Creole singing a short verse and a chorus about love, often teasing or suggestive
near: Don Azpiazú and His Havana Casino Orchestra
The Cuban son-pregón itself, played by a Havana dance orchestra with horns; twoubadou takes such songs (Haitiando sings this one in Kreyòl) to a small Haitian guitar combo
Ensemble Aux Calebasses, Nemours Jean Baptiste & Louis Lahens
Nemours Jean-Baptiste's dance-band compas: a steady electric-era dance groove with a larger band, not the acoustic guitar-and-voices serenade
